idiom_name: object with a dedicated lock member and a published lock accessor
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep the state private, hold the lock in a dedicated lock object (or a lock-typed field), publish it through an accessor, and document the invariant it guards plus the order in which several such locks are acquired. Every collaborator acquires through the language's scoped guard or with-style helper so that all exit paths release; acquisition mode (blocking, timed, try) and kind (mutex, recursive, read-write, no-op) are configuration rather than hard-coded. Where the language can bind the data to the lock (Rust's Mutex<T>, Swift's Synchronization.Mutex) prefer that binding, because it removes the option of forgetting the lock.
code_sketch:
account = LockableAccount()      # state + published lock

guard = account.publish_lock().acquire()   # or: with lock: / withLock { }
try:
    account.read()               # read ...
    account.update(value)        # ... and write: one critical section
finally:
    guard.release()

# the published lock is policy: mutex | recursive | read-write | no-op
pitfalls: Publishing the lock while leaving a back door to the state (raw getters, copies, static access) leaves the object unprotected.
Bare acquire/release pairs without a scoped guard leak the lock on every early return and exception path.
Acquiring several published locks in different orders deadlocks: the order must be one documented global order.
Holding the published lock across I/O, callbacks or foreign calls turns a short critical section into a stall.
Copying the lockable object: in value-semantics languages the lock is a field; copying the object copies the lock — two independent locks guard the same state, breaking exclusion entirely.

Recursive locking on a non-recursive mutex: attempting to re-enter a mutex from the same thread causes deadlock or undefined behaviour; verify the published lock kind matches the recursion profile of all callers.

Spurious wakeups on Condition variables: condition waits must always run in a loop that re-checks the predicate; a single if-check can proceed when the condition is still false, violating the invariant.

Not releasing on panic: in languages where a panic unwinds (Rust, C++ with noexcept-false), a lock held across a panic is not released unless the guard implements Drop (RAII) or a defer/finally unwinds it. Always pair the lock with a scope-bound guard that drops on any exit path.

Lock-free read races: some designs publish a lock but also expose raw fields or relaxed atomics without going through the lock; a reader that bypasses the lock creates a data race even if writes always use the lock.

Wrong move: expose the object's intrinsic monitor to arbitrary callers -> untrusted code can hold it indefinitely, causing contention or deadlock -> instead publish a dedicated lock only to trusted collaborators, or keep synchronization private when no compound operation is required.

Wrong move: treat a timed try-lock timeout as if the critical section was entered -> proceeding without the guard breaks the object's invariant -> instead branch explicitly on acquisition failure and retry, abort, or return a safe result.

Wrong move: wait on a condition backed by a different lock than the predicate -> notifications and predicate visibility are no longer synchronized with the guarded state -> instead associate the condition with the same published lock and re-check the predicate in a loop.
